headings.title: Introduction and Structural Organization
headings.content: Compact bone, also known as cortical bone, forms the dense and sturdy exterior layer of all bones, providing a protective shield and structural framework for the entire human body. While it appears solid to the naked eye, it is a highly organized, living tissue designed to withstand heavy mechanical loads, particularly the compressive and bending forces experienced by long bones in the limbs. In the Nigerian clinical setting, healthcare providers frequently observe the strength of this tissue when managing traumatic fractures resulting from motor vehicle accidents. Understanding this hard outer shell is essential for recognizing how bones heal and maintain structural integrity throughout life.

headings.title: Microscopic Anatomy: The Osteon
headings.content:
The structural unit of compact bone is the **osteon**, or **Haversian system**, which resembles a set of microscopic cylinders nested inside one another. Each osteon consists of several key structural features:

- **Haversian canal**: The central channel running longitudinally through the core of the osteon, housing small blood vessels and nerve fibers.
- **Lamellae**: Concentric rings of calcified extracellular matrix that surround the central canal, providing torsional strength.
- **Lacunae**: Small cavities situated at the boundaries of adjacent lamellae that house mature bone cells.
- **Canaliculi**: Tiny, radiating fluid-filled canals that connect the lacunae to each other and to the central canal, forming a vital transport network.

headings.title: Cellular Components
headings.content:
Compact bone houses four distinct types of bone cells, each playing a specialized role in tissue maintenance, repair, and remodeling throughout a person's life.

- **Osteogenic cells**: Stem cells derived from mesenchyme that divide and differentiate into bone-forming cells.
- **Osteoblasts**: Active cells responsible for synthesizing and secreting the organic components of the bone matrix.
- **Osteocytes**: Mature bone cells enclosed within lacunae that monitor and maintain the surrounding mineralized matrix.
- **Osteoclasts**: Large, multinucleated cells originating from white blood cell lineages that break down bone tissue during remodeling.

headings.title: Extracellular Matrix and Mineralization
headings.content: The extracellular matrix of compact bone is unique because it is both organic and inorganic, creating a material that resists both tension and compression. Approximately one-third of the matrix is organic, consisting mainly of **collagen fibers** and ground substance, which give the bone flexibility and tensile strength. The remaining two-thirds is inorganic, composed primarily of **hydroxyapatite crystals**—complex salts of calcium phosphate. As these mineral salts deposit upon the collagen framework, they harden the tissue. An exam pitfall is assuming bone is entirely dead mineral rock; in reality, this dynamic composite matrix undergoes continuous turnover.

headings.title: Vascular Supply and Volkmann's Canals
headings.content: Because the mineralized matrix of compact bone is impenetrable to simple diffusion, the tissue requires a dedicated vascular network. Blood vessels and nerves travel from the periosteum into the bone through **Volkmann's canals** (also known as perforating canals). Unlike Haversian canals, which run vertically along the axis of an osteon, Volkmann's canals run horizontally or obliquely, interconnecting adjacent Haversian canals and linking the internal bone marrow cavity with the outer periosteum. This interconnected highway ensures that every living osteocyte receives a continuous supply of oxygen and essential nutrients.

headings.title: Comparison with Spongy Bone
headings.content:
| Feature | Compact Bone | Spongy Bone |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Location** | Outer layer of all bones, shaft of long bones | Interior of bones, epiphyses of long bones |
| **Structural Unit** | Osteon (Haversian system) | Trabeculae (lattice-like network) |
| **Density and Weight** | Dense, heavy, and solid | Porous, lightweight, honeycomb-like |
| **Primary Function** | Weight-bearing, protection, resistance to bending | Shock absorption, housing red bone marrow |
